title: Job 24:1–12
context: Job continues his reply, now turning from the search for God in chapter 23 to a hard question and a catalogue: why are times not laid up by the Almighty, and why do those who know him not see his days? Job then describes people who move landmarks, seize flocks, drive off the donkey of the fatherless, take the widow’s ox, push the needy aside, and leave the poor to hunt food like wild donkeys, to lie naked in the cold, and to carry sheaves while hungry. From the city the wounded cry out, “yet God doesn’t regard the folly.” The speech is Job’s lament and protest, not a finished theodicy. The oppressors are they, not a confession of the sins Eliphaz listed in 22:5–9; Job’s picture of the poor stands nearer to his later self-description in 29:12–17 and chapter 31 than to Eliphaz’s charges. Those accounts are to be named, not blended. Both traditions read the unit as a protest against visible injustice and against God’s apparent delay, without a party contrast over the catalogue itself.

verses.text: “Why aren’t times laid up by the Almighty? Why don’t those who know him see his days?
verses.arminianNotes:
Job asks, “Why aren’t times laid up by the Almighty? Why don’t those who know him see his days?” The questions concern judgment: why has the Almighty not stored up times, and why do those who know him not see his days? Job is asking why the days of reckoning are not visible. The questions are protest, not a denial that God exists or knows, and they should not be read as open-theist ignorance in God; Job’s complaint is that those days are not seen, not that God has no knowledge of the way men take (23:10).

Arminian readers hear a real cry about the hiddenness of judgment, a question asked in faith and in pain, not a conclusion that God will never act.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the laid-up times and the unseen days as Job’s protest over delay, God still named as the Almighty, the days still called his.

Both traditions keep the verse as lament over apparent inaction, not as a doctrine that God has no times of his own.

verses.text: There are people who remove the landmarks. They violently take away flocks, and feed them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“There are people who remove the landmarks. They violently take away flocks, and feed them.” The catalogue begins with stolen boundaries and stolen flocks, a public, violent injustice. Job is describing what such people do, not confessing that he has done it. The contrast with Eliphaz’s charges in 22:5–9 may be noted; it should not be turned into a forced harmony.

Arminian readers take the moved landmarks and the taken flocks as a real report of oppression Job has seen, the first items in a list that will grow heavier.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the violence as Job names it, a description of what the wicked do in the land, not a coded admission of his own guilt.

Both traditions keep the speaker and the “they” clear, and invent no contrast over the crimes listed.

verses.text: They drive away the donkey of the fatherless, and they take the widow’s ox for a pledge.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They drive away the donkey of the fatherless, and they take the widow’s ox for a pledge.” The fatherless and the widow are now the victims, their animals taken, the ox taken as a pledge. Eliphaz had accused Job of taking pledges and of breaking the arms of the fatherless (22:6, 22:9). Job’s “they” points the other way. The two pictures should stand side by side, unharmonized.

Arminian readers hear Job naming the very wrongs Eliphaz had pinned on him, and pinning them on others, a protest, not a confession.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set this verse beside 22:6 and 22:9, and later beside 29:12–17 and chapter 31, without blending the voices into one account.

Both traditions refuse to treat Job’s catalogue as Eliphaz’s case proved.

verses.text: They turn the needy out of the way. The poor of the earth all hide themselves.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They turn the needy out of the way. The poor of the earth all hide themselves.” The needy are pushed aside, and the poor hide. The land is made unsafe for the weak. Job’s sympathy is with those who hide, not with those who turn them out.

Arminian readers take the hidden poor as a real social fact in Job’s protest, the weak disappearing from the path because the strong have taken it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the needy turned aside and the poor in hiding, a lament over a public wrong, not a theory about poverty in general.

Both traditions stay with the victims Job names, and invent no contrast over the hiding.

verses.text: Behold, as wild donkeys in the desert, they go out to their work, seeking diligently for food. The wilderness yields them bread for their children.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, as wild donkeys in the desert, they go out to their work, seeking diligently for food. The wilderness yields them bread for their children.” The poor, it seems, are the ones now compared to wild donkeys, hunting food in the desert so that their children may eat. The image is of hard, exposed labor, not of crime. The exact antecedent of “they” in a catalogue can shift; the notes take the verse as continuing the poor, which the food for children most naturally suggests, and they do not assert a reconstruction if a reader hears the subject differently.

Arminian readers hear a grim diligence, parents seeking food in the wilderness, a picture meant to move the hearer, not to accuse the poor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the desert work and the children’s bread as Job’s description of need, hedged as to any tighter identification of every they and not turned into a different scene than the one WEB gives.

Both traditions refuse to over-specify the syntax, and they invent no contrast over the image.

verses.text: They cut their food in the field. They glean the vineyard of the wicked.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They cut their food in the field. They glean the vineyard of the wicked.” The poor cut food in the field and glean in the vineyard of the wicked. They eat from the edges of what others own, including the wicked. The verse is a further stroke in the same picture of want, not a charge that gleaning itself is theft.

Arminian readers take the cutting and the gleaning as survival under others’ power, work that still leaves them in the next verses poorly clothed and cold.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear field and vineyard as the places where the poor must take their food, a detail of oppression’s ordinary day, not a side lesson in agriculture.

Both traditions keep the verse in the catalogue and invent no contrast over the gleaning.

verses.text: They lie all night naked without clothing, and have no covering in the cold.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They lie all night naked without clothing, and have no covering in the cold.” The line is stark and should be told with restraint: the poor spend the night unclothed, with no covering in the cold. Eliphaz had said Job stripped the naked of their clothing (22:6). Job describes the naked as others’ victims. The two claims are to be named, not merged.

Arminian readers hear a real exposure in the cold, a suffering Job reports in protest, not a sin he is admitting.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also set the unclothed night beside 22:6, and later beside Job’s oaths about clothing the needy in chapter 31, without forcing one account to swallow the other.

Both traditions report the cold and the lack of covering soberly, without graphic addition.

verses.text: They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for lack of a shelter.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for lack of a shelter.” Rain and bare rock complete the exposure: they have no shelter, so they hold to the rock. The protest remains concrete and unadorned.

Arminian readers take the wet bodies and the embraced rock as Job’s picture of people without a house, a further cry over what is done to the poor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the mountain showers and the rock as the shelter that is no shelter, Job still describing, not yet answering his own question of 24:1.

Both traditions keep the verse restrained and invent no contrast over the image.

verses.text: There are those who pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor,
verses.arminianNotes:
“There are those who pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor,” The cruelty is now named at the point of the family: the fatherless taken from the breast, a pledge taken from the poor. The verse should be reported as Job gives it, with pastoral restraint, without expansion. It is among the hardest lines in the catalogue, and it is still about those who, not about Job’s own hand.

Arminian readers hear a protest against a violent taking of children and a harsh pledge, evils Job is placing at others’ doors.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the plucked fatherless and the pledge as Job’s accusation of the oppressors, to be read against Eliphaz’s charges and against chapter 31, not as a confession.

Both traditions tell the line soberly and invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: so that they go around naked without clothing. Being hungry, they carry the sheaves.
verses.arminianNotes:
The result is that “they go around naked without clothing. Being hungry, they carry the sheaves.” The poor are again unclothed, and they carry sheaves while hungry: they handle food they do not eat. The injustice is in the ordinary work of the harvest.

Arminian readers take the nakedness and the hungry carrying of sheaves as a real inversion, labor beside food that is not theirs to eat.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear sheaves on the shoulders of the hungry, a detail Job stacks with 24:7, the same want continuing into the field work.

Both traditions leave the picture as it stands and invent no contrast over the harvest.

verses.text: They make oil within the walls of these men. They tread wine presses, and suffer thirst.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They make oil within the walls of these men. They tread wine presses, and suffer thirst.” They press oil and tread grapes inside the owners’ walls, and they go thirsty. Drink is made by people who have none. The protest is still economic and bodily, not a parable in need of decoding.

Arminian readers hear oil and wine produced by the thirsty and the poor, a further unadorned charge against the owners Job has in view.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the walls, the presses, and the thirst as Job’s report of labor without its fruit, part of the same catalogue, not a separate riddle.

Both traditions refuse to allegorize the oil and the wine, and they invent no contrast over the thirst.

verses.text: From out of the populous city, men groan. The soul of the wounded cries out, yet God doesn’t regard the folly.
verses.arminianNotes:
“From out of the populous city, men groan. The soul of the wounded cries out, yet God doesn’t regard the folly.” The scene widens to the city: groaning, a cry from the wounded, and then the hard close, that God does not regard the folly. Job is saying that the cry seems unanswered. This is the protest of 24:1 now in a single clause, and it should be handled soberly, as lament, not as a settled doctrine that God never sees or never will act. Job has already said that God knows the way he takes (23:10).

Arminian readers hear a real cry over apparent disregard, a complaint that does not cancel God’s knowledge or reduce God to a spectator who cannot act.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take “doesn’t regard the folly” as Job’s protest over delay and hiddenness, not as the book’s last word on God’s government, and not as a claim that God is truly inattentive in himself.

Both traditions keep the verse as lament, share the refusal to make it a finished theodicy, and invent no contrast over the wording.
